about: Hand-graded expectations for judge-calibration rows. Each answer was read against its own retrieved contexts and every claim traced to supporting text, so the human faithfulness expectation is 1.000 throughout. Rationales cite where support was found without reproducing the source text. answer_relevancy has no defensible human scalar (it measures embedding distance between the question and questions reverse-generated from the answer, not answer quality), so it is deliberately unlabelled.
known_limitations: EVERY label is 1.000, so this set has no negative examples. A judge that returned 'faithful' unconditionally would score a perfect mean-absolute-error against it. Judge-vs-human agreement computed from these rows therefore measures FALSE-NEGATIVE rate only, not accuracy, and cannot distinguish a more correct judge from a more lenient one. Add rows with genuinely unsupported answers before using this comparison to choose a judge.

The rows are not a random sample: four of six were selected because the incumbent judge disagreed with manual inspection, and two are positive controls. Stability and agreement figures derived from them are biased and must not be generalised to the full 90-row baseline.

labels.rationale: Single-claim answer; the claim is a near-verbatim restatement of one sentence in retrieved context rank 1. Baseline judge returned 0.000.

Both the per-day death rate and the MTTF range appear in retrieved context rank 1. Prior runs scored 1.000/1.000/0.667, but those inputs were NOT identical — the generated answer differed in the 0.667 run, so that spread was generation variance, not judge variance. Included here to be re-measured under fixed inputs.
